reviewText: As you're probably aware, the Notorious B.I.G.'s life was tragically cut short in March 1997, and his final album, the double-disc "Life After Death," was released as scheduled mere weeks later. "Life After Death" is stunning in more ways than one. In a word, this album is epic. Over the course of two discs and 24 tracks, Biggie compiled a spectacle of a collection, with big-time productions, A-list collaborations, and hit singles. More so than his landbreaking debut Ready to Die, which was overall a grimier, humbler approach to a masterpiece, "Life After Death" is a big-budget, remarkable project to behold. Where his debut was filled with rags-to-riches tales of hustling and crime, the change his newfound wealth brought to his lifestyle is refelcted in his sophomore effort. The glamorous tales of his lavish lifestyle are highlighted in club tracks and party jams, but lyrically and technically he is as good here as he ever was. The spooky storytelling, hilarious punchlines, wide-eyed philosophy, and chilling threats are at their most effective. Technically, he is even better than before, utilizing an impeccable flow and vocabulary. Probably most stunning though, is the dramatic way in which he talks about death, given that he would die before this album would even be released. Whether referring to others or himself, his talk of the afterlife and judgement is among the most interesting and amazing parts this album has to offer. The tracklist is long and split between many types of tracks, including great radio-friendly singles, grimy street anthems, chilling narratives, seductive tracks for the ladies, and club songs. But somehow, he was able to pull all of these different intangibles together for another fluent masterpiece. Sean Combs and Easy Mo Bee anchor a production team that also includes such big names as Clark Kent, RZA, Kay Gee, Buckwild, and DJ Premier for production that lives up to the MC in every manner. "Life After Death" is another incredible hip hop album and much to behold.Following the intro, the first disc opens with "Somebody's Gotta Die," a hard, grimy narrative with production and lyricism that will bring to mind multiple tracks from the debut. The light-hearted "Hypnotize" is an unforgettable single that remains in heavy radio rotation even today, a bass-heavy party jam with funny punchlines and a silly hook. DJ Premier produced "Kick in the Door," a solid, upbeat track, and R. Kelly guests on the popular "F... You Tonight," a seductive love song with great production. Fellow (then) Bad Boy artists The LOX collaborate for "Last Day," a hard-hitting streets cut, and Jay-Z and Angela Winbush are the guests for the lavish anthem "I Love the Dough." This song is a definite highlight, the production is rich, upbeat, and very funky, and the happy yet thoughtful song is lots of fun to listen to. "What's Beef?" assesses the state of rivalry both in hip hop and urban life, lyrically a strong piece. Biggie's most famous single comes next on the tracklist, "Mo Money Mo Problems," a true anthem featuring Ma$e, Puff Daddy, and a sample from Diana Ross. This song is ingeniously produced, utilizing the sample brilliantly, and the joyful verses combined with great production equal a true musical triumph for the trio, the song that epitomized Bad Boy Records. The rough "N... Bleed" and the clever "I Got a Story to Tell," the tale of a late-night escapade over a nice beat, close disc one.Disc two opens with a bang, the epic six-minute Bone Thugs-N-Harmony collaboration "Notorious Thugs." This song is a true classic, with a phenomenal, Cleveland-styled beat and well-written, rapid-fire verses from the MCs. 112 provides the R&B; hook and bridge for the sad "Miss U," which flexes great production, and his young protege Lil Kim provides a memorable appearance on the funny "Another." At this point, the classic joints come one after another. "Going Back to Cali" is an excellent, upbeat funker with the luxurious tales of laidback life on the west coast. DJ Premier's masterful production on "Ten Crack Commandments" provides a backdrop for Biggie to drop wisdom from his days as a hustler. "Playa Hater" is the funniest song on the album, where Biggie sings like a silly soul singer, hilariously informing a victim, "You've been robbed." The light and funky "Nasty Boy" precedes another dramatic 112 collaboration, which opens with words of motivation from none other than his mother. My favorite song on the whole album is "The World Is Filled...," which features Too Short and Puff Daddy. This song doesn't stand out among the epic tracks here, but I've always found the laidback production and harsh philosophy relaxing. The last three songs are the most stunning, epic, and dramatic, dealing with death. "My Downfall" samples Run-DMC for a chilling chorus, a very well done and effective song. The infamous Wu-Tang beatcraft the RZA produced "Long Kiss Goodnight," an eerie threat to a backstabber with an excellent chorus. Most chilling of all, though, is the closer "You're Nobody (Til Somebody Kills You)." This song is so chilling because the words he preached here proved so ironically true, very sadly. The beat is perfect and this song is absolutely chilling."Life After Death" is dramatic and epic first and foremost, a phenomenal work that tragically was the last we will ever see of the great Christopher Wallace, one of the finest MCs to ever rock the mic. This album had such a wide influence, it's interesting for me to see how many of today's rappers are still recycling lines and beats from this album even ten years later. Unlike many listeners, I find this album at least every bit as fulfilling as his classic debut, and I recommend it to any hip hop fan.

Where his debut was filled with rags-to-riches tales of hustling and crime, the change his newfound wealth brought to his lifestyle is refelcted in his sophomore effort. The glamorous tales of his lavish lifestyle are highlighted in club tracks and party jams, but lyrically and technically he is as good here as he ever was. The spooky storytelling, hilarious punchlines, wide-eyed philosophy, and chilling threats are at their most effective. Technically, he is even better than before, utilizing an impeccable flow and vocabulary. Probably most stunning though, is the dramatic way in which he talks about death, given that he would die before this album would even be released. Whether referring to others or himself, his talk of the afterlife and judgement is among the most interesting and amazing parts this album has to offer. somehow, he was able to pull all of these different intangibles together for another fluent masterpiece. "Life After Death" is another incredible hip hop album and much to behold.Following the intro, the first disc opens with "Somebody's Gotta Die," a hard, grimy narrative with production and lyricism that will bring to mind multiple tracks from the debut. The light-hearted "Hypnotize" is an unforgettable single that remains in heavy radio rotation even today, a bass-heavy party jam with funny punchlines and a silly hook. DJ Premier produced "Kick in the Door," a solid, upbeat track, and R. Kelly guests on the popular "F... You Tonight," a seductive love song with great production. Fellow (then) Bad Boy artists The LOX collaborate for "Last Day," a hard-hitting streets cut, and Jay-Z and Angela Winbush are the guests for the lavish anthem "I Love the Dough." This song is a definite highlight, the production is rich, upbeat, and very funky, and the happy yet thoughtful song is lots of fun to listen to. assesses the state of rivalry both in hip hop and urban life, lyrically a strong piece. Biggie's most famous single comes next on the tracklist, "Mo Money Mo Problems," a true anthem featuring Ma$e, Puff Daddy, and a sample from Diana Ross. Bleed" and the clever "I Got a Story to Tell," the tale of a late-night escapade over a nice beat, close disc one.Disc two opens with a bang, the epic six-minute Bone Thugs-N-Harmony collaboration "Notorious Thugs." This song is a true classic, with a phenomenal, Cleveland-styled beat and well-written, rapid-fire verses from the MCs. 112 provides the R&B; hook and bridge for the sad "Miss U," which flexes great production, and his young protege Lil Kim provides a memorable appearance on the funny "Another." At this point, the classic joints come one after another. "Going Back to Cali" is an excellent, upbeat funker with the luxurious tales of laidback life on the west coast. DJ Premier's masterful production on "Ten Crack Commandments" provides a backdrop for Biggie to drop wisdom from his days as a hustler. My favorite song on the whole album is "The World Is Filled...," which features Too Short and Puff Daddy. This song doesn't stand out among the epic tracks here, but I've always found the laidback production and harsh philosophy relaxing. The last three songs are the most stunning, epic, and dramatic, dealing with death. "My Downfall" samples Run-DMC for a chilling chorus, a very well done and effective song. The infamous Wu-Tang beatcraft the RZA produced "Long Kiss Goodnight," an eerie threat to a backstabber with an excellent chorus. Most chilling of all, though, is the closer "You're Nobody (Til Somebody Kills You)." This song is so chilling because the words he preached here proved so ironically true, very sadly. The beat is perfect and this song is absolutely chilling."Life After Death" is dramatic and epic first and foremost, a phenomenal work that tragically was the last we will ever see of the great Christopher Wallace, one of the finest MCs to ever rock the mic. This album had such a wide influence, it's interesting for me to see how many of today's rappers are still recycling lines and beats from this album even ten years later. Unlike many listeners, I find this album at least every bit as fulfilling as his classic debut, and I recommend it to any hip hop fan.

reviewText: Country music--and, largely, rock n roll--would not be what it is today without the teaming of Waylon Jennings and Billy Joe Shaver.  The result of their combined efforts--the hostility, the respect--is HONKY TONK HEROES, an album of pure, unfiltered music that strikes straight to the heart.Songs such as the title track, "Black Rose," and "Ain't No God in Mexico" use upbeat rhythms and pounding guitars to convey their serious messages; other tracks, such as "Old Five and Dimers" and "Low Down Freedom," are so haunting you'll shiver.  Shaver's songwriting is nearly unparalleled in music history, and, let's face it, nobody could sing a tune quite like Waylon Jennings.  HONKY TONK HEROES is a classic, pure and simple--a true classic.

reviewText: Im SO ICY.....SO ICY!!!!!!!Hey...Gucci Mane has become an underground sensation in the big city of ATL with his summer time hit So Icy featuring Young Jeezy & Boo (Another version has some other guy rappin on it too but he was taken off.).  Quick to capitalize on his sudden popularity he cut a video that has been getting heavy airplay on BET and prepared the album, Trap House, to be released on his independent record label BigCatRecords (also the home of recent ATOWn sensation Maceo, who's hit record HO SIT DOWN has become an anthem in the city of ATL.).  However, Gucci Mane's career may be over as quickly as he started as he and Young Jeezy ( the next to blow out the south...TI status & popularity down here...Trap Or Die get that...as well as Boyz N Da Hood - Dem Boyz) have developed a disliking for each other and he's facing a murder charge (I won't go into details you can find it on the Internet somewhere if interested).Nonetheless, Trap House has been released.  Although Gucci Mane isn't a great rapper he's better than the majority of independent acts.  And even though his lyrics are sometimes wack, he can come up with clever lines and sayings and catchy hooks.  His beats are also dirty underground ATown style, the same as his flow.  His lyrical content is the usual women, cars, money, hustling, flossin, killing, trappin (that's pretty much what everyone raps about) but he delivers it in an  entertaining way and that's what I look for when I purchase a cd. Overall Gucci Mane delivers with what he's supposed to; a hot summer album with some feel good songs perfect for ridin.  If you like dirty south music, especially that coming from the ATown go ahead and pick that up.  3.5 Stars

reviewText: I have to admitt, it took time for Sade's work to grow on me. But back in 2000 when "By Your Side" came out, I started to get hooked and after purchasing "Lovers Rock," I went for this. Now, don't be expecting an album full of variety. Sade has always been a consistent artist and her work sticks to the smooth jazz/R&B vein, but at the same time, it's part of what makes her so great. You pretty much know what you're getting."Best of Sade" captures her best singles ranging from 1985's "Diamond Life" to 1992's "Love Deluxe." My favorite Sade song and her biggest pop hit is the classic "Smooth Operator" which represents everything that makes her so great. Her other big hit is here also which is the enjoyable "Sweetest Taboo." The other songs are for the most part just as good from the haunting "Jezebel" and "Is It A Crime" to the jazzy "Hang On To Your Love." Sade also had considerable hits with "No Ordinary Love" and "Paradise." Another one of personal Sade favorites is present here also and that's "Please Send Me Someone To Love."This is a great relaxation album. Sade is definitely a master at her craft. Smooth vocals, mesmerizing songs...a good buy. Give it time and you'll love it. And if you like Sade, I also recommend Enya.

reviewText: In 1979, Heaven took back a gift that was loaned to us for only a short time.  That gift was Minnie Riperton.  Although she is gone, in the physical sense at least, the voice of this 'Perfect Angel' and her legacy live on.This CD is filled with playful songs, seductive songs, sing-a-long songs, and love songs.  The sexiest joint on this CD is "Can You Feel What I'm Saying", which is also a song that makes me feel a lot better after a bad day.  Minnie's voice has a way of making you want to smile, sing, cry- all at the same time.  The child-like innocence in her voice is what makes her sound playful, yet the intensity and depth in it, makes her sound like a seductive siren."Here We Go", "Memory Lane", "Inside My Love" and "Perfect Angel" are all gems, along with other tracks, but there is something about "Simple Things" that is almost angelic.  The jazzy/latin sounding rhythm makes you want to sway from side to side.  And in the song, "Take My Breath Away", (which sounds like Donny Hathaway singing in the background) she sings of things that are all around us like, "a tree/ a rock, a cloud/ a sky blue day", which we take for granted, but in them, she saw them as things that 'took her breath away'.May God bless the soul of Minnie Riperton, the same way she blessed our ears with wonderful music, and our hearts with her very presence.

reviewText: Their self-titled debut would prove to be Rage Against the Machine's best effort, though they hardly slipped over the ensuing years and albums.  This is a classic in the truest sense of the word:  it begs you to pull it out of your collection at least 2-3 times a year, and it represents some of the best music from its time and place.  RATM reminds you that the best music SAYS SOMETHING, whether it's politically-motivated or just something the artist feels the need to share with their audience.  Rage's blend of incendiary metal riffing (courtesy of Tom Morello's groundbreaking guitar work), pounding drums, and scream-in-your-ear agenda-pushing lyrics was powerful, unique, and uncompromising.  This is an essential album for anyone that listens to message-heavy music.

reviewText: I remember seeing the video for Burning Heart on MTV back in the day, and loved the song. However, whenever I saw the album, I failed to pick it up and it faded into obscurity. Then I got involved with Picture and learned that Bert Heerink was their vocalist on some of their later 80's work. That piqued my interest again and I kept an eye out for anything by Vandenberg.I saw Adrian when he played with Whitesnake in the 80's in Spain and he played guitar and keyboards. I remember at the show, he hit a wrong chord on the keyboards and got a laugh from Dave Coverdale.I found the vinyl version in a record shop in Las Vegas in 2009 and burned it to CD. I've been playing it and it rocks!The songs are well crafted and would fit just nicely with harder-edged hair metal. There is something more here than just spandex and hair spray. Adrian plays a mean guitar, his solos are not gratuitous, and his composing skills are top-notch. Bert Heerink's voice is great and an excellent fit for the songs. Overall, this is a great album.My only criticism is that as good as it is, it is a touch generic. However, it is still good, and besides Burning Heart, I keep thinking of the line from the song Wait, "Wait 'till the **** hits the fan." Good stuff. Highly recommended for lovers of 80s rock.

reviewText: I can't describe how wonderful this recording is, but I'll try.  Whether you like bluegrass or not, if you appreciate good singing, good playing, and wonderful melodies, this CD is for you.  Many people have talked about how relaxing, soothing and peaceful (not to mention fun!) this collection is.  It's that and more.  These are songs that you will find yourself singing, humming, and thinking about after just a few listens.  Alison does a wide range of covers, including the title track from the Foundations, a song by Bad Company ("Oh Atlanta"), and a wonderful version of the Beatles' "I Will."  Now about Alison Krauss...You can read here and in many other places about the enormous talent Alison has been blessed with.  That is obvious in the initial hearing of the CD.  I appreciate the talent, but even more I appreciate the love that she has for music.  I've seen and heard many performers in several different genres of music, but it is becoming a true rarity to encounter artists who really, truly love what they do.  You can tell that Alison Krauss (and Union Station) has a geniune joy in doing what she does.  It comes across in the music.  That joy of singing, performing, communicating with an audience is sadly lacking with most artists today.  Too many artists (some who once had this joy and lost it somewhere along the way) are in music for all the wrong reasons...money, fame, you name it.  Krauss will have none of it.  She still records for Rounder Records, a relatively small label, even though she's had offers from the big labels.  She refuses to perform in big arena concerts because she would lose the close connection she has with her audience.  I admire her for her decisions and for her love of her craft.  Take one listen to this CD and I think you'll agree.

reviewText: After listening to this album for a while, I have to wonder when Julie Miller is going to put another album out. This is some amazing stuff. The music is very heartfelt and endearing, very personal and revealing. BROKEN THINGS opens with the wonderful "Ride The Wind To Me", which has a great chorus and overall feeling to it. "I Know Why The River Runs" is a really, really beautiful song that means a lot to me. Something about the lyrics and the structure of the song, it's remarkable. "I Need You" is a nice little rocker. "I Still Cry" is a remarkable ballad, with great lyrics and it's just quite sad. The title track is another favorite of mine, it's very sad but a very honest song that's relatable. "All My Tears" is another standout, I love Emmylou Harris' version of this song as well. Lee Ann Womack has recorded a handful of these songs including "I Know Why The River Runs", "I Need You" and "Orphan Train". Other highlights on this amazing album include "Maggie", "Strange Lover" and "The Speed of Light". If you haven't heard of Julie Miller, you should check out this album and her BLUE PONY album. She has a unique voice and is one of the best songwriters I've heard from in a long time.

The music is very heartfelt and endearing, very personal and revealing. BROKEN THINGS opens with the wonderful "Ride The Wind To Me", which has a great chorus and overall feeling to it. "I Know Why The River Runs" is a really, really beautiful song that means a lot to me. Something about the lyrics and the structure of the song, it's remarkable. "I Need You" is a nice little rocker. "I Still Cry" is a remarkable ballad, with great lyrics and it's just quite sad. The title track is another favorite of mine, it's very sad but a very honest song that's relatable. "All My Tears" is another standout, I love Emmylou Harris' version of this song as well. Lee Ann Womack has recorded a handful of these songs including "I Know Why The River Runs", "I Need You" and "Orphan Train". Other highlights on this amazing album include "Maggie", "Strange Lover" and "The Speed of Light". If you haven't heard of Julie Miller, you should check out this album and her BLUE PONY album. She has a unique voice and is one of the best songwriters I've heard from in a long time.

reviewText: "12 Gardens Live" is a two-disc souvenir of Billy Joel's recent lengthy stand at Madison Square Garden. He gallops through selections from his entire career, mixing his pop standards with a few fan favorites and one or two bizarro choices ("Great Wall of China"? Really?)As a live album, it's not going to win over any music fan whose opinion of Billy Joel is "undecided." It's competent and enthusiastic (for the most part), but it just has that "for the fans" feeling about it.Which is fine, isn't it? I'm one of them, and I like having this in my collection...I wish I was there, in fact.But the songs are sometimes rushed (Piano Man), ponderous (Goodnight Saigon) or perfunctory (more than one).Sometimes his piano playing is thrilling in its' virtuosity (LOVE the piano break in "Scenes From an Italian...", and the prelude to "Angry Young Man" is always fun to listen to...) but other times it is kinda sloppy.That sort of stuff gives the album a bit of character and realism, but when the other tunes sound so impeccable, it feels a bit uneven.Any fan will have songs they would prefer on the set list, and will also have songs that they never really have to hear again. I'm pretty much done with "Zanzibar."What I really hope is that there is some video document of these shows...THAT'S probably the best representation of what a total party these concerts must have been.C'mon Billy. Give us one, uncut, killer show from MSG on DVD. Please?

reviewText: Few weeks ago I bought this disk, after buying Mezz, Blue Lines and 100th Window a long time ago. Why didn't I buy it sooner, you ask? For starters, I always wanted another CD first in stead of this one, I always moved it. And also because pretty much all the critici gave this album a bad review, saying the only worthly songs on it are 'Protection' and 'Karmacoma'. So with low expectations I bought this and putted in the disk-player. First there were 'Protection' and 'Karmacoma' wich I already knew they were great, so no surprises yet. So when 'Karmacoma' ended I was preparing myself hearing really crappy and lame music. But it wasn't... to be honoust it was really good, extraordinary. Near the end I knew it for sure: Protection is better than Blue Lines. Blue Lines was revolutionary and very good, but it sounds so dated and Protection is more exciting with its fascinating and sometimes even strange sound.'Protection' and 'Karmacoma' are the best tracks on the album and 2 of MA's toppers, while 'Protection' has very soft, fragile vocals and smooth instruments, 'Karmacoma' sounds very Jamacian with its rap vocals (Normally I don't like rap but it seems to work very well on Massive Attack-tracks), I can hardly choose wich one is the best between those 2 songs. 'Three' has a really fascinating intro, and a male voice who is always repeating the same line, and beautiful female vocals, that all together makes this another stand out.'Weather Storm' is a very nice jazzy instrumential with a playful piano and decent beats. 'Spying Glass' is by far the weirdest track on this album. A strange combination between jazzy instruments and chilling vocals makes this track very special, but not all listeners might like it. 'Better Things' has some nice jazzy bass-lines and a quit beautiful melody. Vocals are not less then amazing again.'Euro Child' is the darkest song on here, but it doesn't lose the jazzy feel on this disk. Dark rap-vocals, with creepy jazz-sounds mixed with quit weird instruments makes this another stand out, my third favourite..Yet another fascinating track, and a single, is 'Sly'. Again an outstanding combination between instrumentents. Vocals are mysterious and the Digiridu's add that little extra a song needs to be good. The strikers give a more classical feel to it.Then we have another instrumential, but this one is more complex and less jazzy than 'Weather Storm'. Synths were used instead of a piano. Good, but I must say, I like 'Weather Storm' better.After 'Heat Miser' I usually start over the album, because the next song isn't really good, it's in my opinion the only disappointement on this disk. Maybe because 'Light My Fire' is just...well...so non-Massive Attack. It has not instruments enough to be a worthy MA-track, it sounds so empty. And live-songs on an album usually don't sound very good anyway.Nevertheless this is an incredible album, better then Blue Lines. Mezzanine is still my favourite, about half an inch ahead of Protection. I might say, Protection makes Mezzanine sound less impressive..

reviewText: Label me surprised. Terrifically surprised. And happily. I had few  positive expectations for this debut solo album by the former co-leader of  Veruca Salt. While that group's two albums held a few pleasures, they were  uneven (to say the  least), and certainly did not suggest in any way that  there was a repressed power popster in their midst.But there was, and  here's the fruit of her newfound liberation. Imagine a cross between Aimee  Mann, Juliana Hatfield and latter-era Bangles, with a dollup of Joan Jett  tossed in for good measure, and you have a good idea of what you'll find  herein.  Catchy-as-heck songs, big budget widescreen production, big  energy, good vibes, good singing, good playing, good gosh. There are a few  duff lyrical couplets ("He likes to try on my clothes but not my  underwear"...ugh) and a few too many coy plays on the word  "blow". Lyrically this ain't Aimee Mann, but that's hardly more  than a quibble when the music is this good...This album is radio  friendly in all the best ways, and Gordon seems more than a bit photogenic.  With any luck this record will lead the charge against the moronic factory  teen pop that kidnapped popular music a few years ago.Now more than  ever, we all need a Nina Gordon at the top of charts.dap

reviewText: What hogwash the few reviewers have given this album. I own all 11 cds from him and "Dear Heather" is definitely above such lows as 1979's "Recent Songs" or 1977's "Death Of A Ladies Man". Is it as sharp as his first three albums? No. Is it as strong as "I'm Your Man" or "The Future"? No. But it definitely has its place in his canon of work.Just keep in mind that before all these bands like Radiohead, Keane, Travis, Snow Patrol, etc. There was Leonard Cohen (even before The Cure). Cohen is virtually without peer at 70 years of age. There are some great songs on "Dear Heather" like "Go No More A-Roving", "Because Of", "The Letters", "Morning Glory", "Villanelle For Our Time", "Dear Heather" and "Nightingale". In fact, "The Letters" and "Villanelle" are two of his finest works. "Dear Heather" is a strange, almost Laurie Anderson-like piece of song that shows, even at 70, Cohen is still willing to take musical risks."Dear Heather" is an unusual mix of modern engineering with an antiquated musical feel (some of the songs are waltzes) and vintage instrumentation (I believe he uses the mouth harp on two different songs!)Overall, I was pleased with this album more than 2001's "Ten New Songs". This one has more musical variety. I find it strange that the few Cohen reviews here are very mixed (as if this album was a radical departure or something?!!) Ridiculous. If you are a Cohen fan, you should buy this and add it to your collection.

reviewText: Double albums can be tricky endeavors. Most of them could have easily been whittled down to a single great album (The Clash's "Sandinista" for example) while other double albums wouldn't be the same if a single track was removed.Stadium Arcadium falls in the latter category.I've been a Peppers fan ever since I first got to hear the Uplift Mofo Party Plan CD and I've been hooked ever since. The only release that I don't care for at all out of their entire catalog was 1995's One Hot Minute, which suffered greatly from one time guitarist Dave Navarro ruining their overall sound (not to mention the songs were awful for the most part).Some people have seriously complained about the more mellow direction that the Peppers have gone in starting with 1999's Californication (which was the return to the fold of guitarist John Frusciante).  People forget that now, these guys are in their mid 40's for the most part.  If you want to hear the in your face youthful aggression of their earlier stuff, then just go back and listen to their earlier stuff. Quit complaining that their new stuff isn't Blood Sugar Sex Magik 2.I'm 31 years old now and in a much, much different place than I was 15 years ago. I'm sure the same is for the Peppers as whole as well. I have found that the Pepper's change in direction to a certain extent over the last couple of albums mirrors my life as I've gotten older.But Stadium Arcadium is kind of a kick in the pants with some tracks harkening back to their older style of music. There's other stuff that is more in the laid back mode of 2002's By The Way, but it still has a bit more vibrancy than the stuff on that otherwise great release did.Cd #1 is a little over 62 minutes in length while CD #2 is just a few seconds shy of topping out at exactly an hour in length.That's a lot of music to digest. But the smorgasbord of styles they gallop through on this release makes this one of the best CD's in quite some time to just sit back, chill out and let the sounds envelop you.Some might argue that this release could have been paired down to a single CD of material, but I wholeheartedly disagree. Every song is a gem.Is this as great of a release as Blood Sugar Sex Magik is? Only time will tell, but I can say that it's their best release since that monumental 1991 classic.
summary: Truly amazing and every song is great.

reviewText: There's something about Shellac that makes you feel whichever of their three lp's you are listening too is the best thing next to crack rocks and puppy dogs. Therefore, it's hard to accurately say which Shellac album is my favorite. However, the one i've listened to the most and for the longest time would be Terraform. There's something about that first song that just weeds out all the pop fans, leaving just us noise addicts in their wake. From there, the album branches into all sorts of distorted disjointed guitar slabs, bass lines that push you up to the edge, and drums that pummel you but leave you begging for one more crash cymbal. Pick this baby up, then get Action Park, then 1000 Hurts, and all on vinyl, because it's Steve's music, what he says goes...

reviewText: The absolute bare-bones essential Elton John - that's what this album is. Containing perhaps his 10 most famous songs - some of the biggest hit singles of the first half of the 1970's - as well as the wonderful album track, Border Song, it is certainly a masterful collection of wonderful songs that will get anyone who hears it hooked on Elton. It contains all of his big hit singles from this period (except for three: ["]Tiny Dancer["] (now enjoying a resurgence in popularity due to its appearance in the movie Almost Famous), ["]Levon["], and ["]The Bitch Is Back["].) Although he has always had many great dedicated album tracks, to most people, Elton John will always be a singles artist. And the singles here are immaculate - wonderful, acutely perfect pop nuggets, from the master. No one other than The Beatles (and even they didn't do it as well) can touch Elton on crafting absolute pop perfection. And these songs are proof. It's a fine place to start if you're looking to dip your toe into the world of Elton John. That said, it by no means gives a full picture of this magnificent and multi-faceted artist. Some of his albums - particularly the sprawling double album Goodbye Yellow Brick Road, still one of my favorite records of all time - have a great feel and mood all their own (four tracks here are excerpted from it), and deserve to be heard on their own. Instead, let this be your ticket to experience more Elton John, in all his immaculate pop greatness.

reviewText: Faithless first came out in 1996 and released what was going to become a classic, "Insomnia" which is a very unique dance track. Faithless is not only about dance however, their music influents changes from song to song, so don't be surprised if you hear something completely diffrent then the the hit single "Insomnia" here. There are also a few diffrent singers on the album. Jamie Catto that is somehow the frontfigure on the outside, Dido with others.Faithless is Rollo and Sister Bliss, Maxi Jazz and Jamie Catto however, the first 2 started of as house producers and were behind some good songs in the early 90's, Faithless is far from a house band even if they are heavy infleunted by dance music."Insomnia" Is a very strange song, it starts with drums and a haunting melody typical for "house" music. Catto starts some slow philophical rapping about life, then after 2 minutes the "hook" arrives which is the "dance melody". "Salva Mea" is simular and one of the best songs on this album, watch out this is a long song aswell. it has some very good dance rthythm, however it's sang by a female aswell. The lead title "Reverence" reminds me abit of Arrested Development. Catto is rapping with some catchy backround beats. "Don't Leave" is sung by a man, with backround choirs. "Angeline" is simular to it, it also includes flutes that sound China influented. For those of you that liked Dido, yeah she appeared on "Flowerstand Man" a typical Dido song. I like "Drifting Away" alot it's slow almost ambient, and very beautiful dance song.For those of you that likes dance music and like artisticm albums that are diffrent from your average dance album, take a look at this almost flawless dance masterpiece. Faithless has it all. They later followed up with the great "Sunday 8pm" and "Outrospective" which i didn't like. This album "Reverence" is highly recommended, it suits amny diffrent kinds of music taste.

reviewText: This album simply rocks. Not in a Rock and Roll fashion, nor a classic 70's or punk 80's fashion. Title TK is the perfect combination between folk and punk, where the atmosphere is created by a revolution of riffs and bass leads. The tone of the record is kept top-notch even if sound quality is meant to be non-digital. I have not heard any of The Breeders last albums yet, but im really impressed with the work theyve done here. The Deal sisters eerie singing and monotone backups are wonderful. I love that whole singing-without-moving-your-tounge-punk thing. The guitars create melodious backup, while the drums are kept below simplicity disregarding the time here and there, lifting the whole basement-type-recording a step.Probably the thing you could condemn about this album is the fact that there are only two types of songs. The gloomy-stmospheric type where voice melodies and bass play the lead roles, and the more edgy and rocking ones, where guitars set the tone, followed by playfull vocals such as "ah-ah-ah-ah."Songs most notable on the record are "Little Fury," the "title track" that sets the atmosphere for the whole record (my personal favourite) guitars here are pretty cool, especially the high toned ones in the background that come out every once in a while, they give te song a whole happy thing. "Too Alive" which is the edgy type of song, "Put on a Side" which resembles some sonic youth musically, but is set aside by the sisters vocals, simple. "Sinister Foxx" the gloomy tipe where the sister's accent is dramatized by a punk-type pronunciation where certain syllables are pronounced tongueless. And last but not least "Huffer" which is the fastest song of the record.Ive found that no matter when i listen to this record it puts me in a lively mood. If punk was meant to get you agressive, this is meant to get you awake. Title TK has proved to be one of the best records of the year, and it certainly has moved up the standards in the alt-scene.My recommendation?This album is a must!

reviewText: What can be said about an album whose lyrics I've memorized after owning it for just one month?On When the Pawn.... that darling of brooding and angst, Fiona Apple, gets even darker than she was on her 1996 debut Tidal.  While Fiona seemed to wallow in sadness and despair on Tidal, she adopts a  wry perspective on love gone wrong on When the Pawn."It won't be  long till you'll be lying limp in your own hands", she disgustedly  tells her ex, on "Limp". She grows even angrier on "Get  Gone", when she realizes that her lover doesn't care about her  ("How many times do I have to say, to get away...get gone"). And  on "Fast As You Can" she warns her prospective lover to be wary  of her fickle ways.One also gets the feeling that Fiona is tired of  having to live up to other people's expectations on "A mistake",  where she slyly croons, "I've acquired quite a taste/for a well-made  mistake". She's also not immune to obsessive love which she deals with  on the wry track "Paper Bag".As well as being a more  lyrically mature album "When the Pawn" also signals Apple's  maturation as a writer of music. The melodies are spare, but intense, and  producer Jon Brion has added more spice and funk to the music than was  present on Tidal.When the Pawn puts to rest any notion of Fiona Apple  being a flash in the pan. It looks like this Angst Girl will be around for  some time to come.

reviewText: This must be the 900th Willie Nelson album with each successive one becoming increasingly formulaic - contrast this album with Red Headed Stranger or Georgia. Musically and vocally competent but lacking anything in the way of fresh sparks. "Grandma's Hands" works only because of the incomparable Mavis Staples - Mr Nelson sounds uncomfortable and his breathless delivery is sub par. Much recycling of the Highwayman publishing catalog - but kudos to Mr Nelson - at 80 years old- a fashion plate, his own station on SiriusXM and regular releases.

reviewText: "Life for Rent," Dido's second album, contains great songs full of lost love, guilt, and hope, all sung by one of the most haunting, delicate and deceptively plain voices in pop music today.  (No flourishes or over-singing on this album!)  Dido's talents are not limited to singing, either writing or co-writing all the songs on the album.  The music ranges from pop songs, including "Life for Rent" and "Stoned," to an almost R&B/funk feel on "Who Makes You Feel" and even a danceable "Sand in My Shoes."  There's even a hidden track that fits well with the rest of the album.  Standout songs:  "White Flag," "Don't Leave Home,"  "Life for Rent," and "See the Sun."

reviewText: I was happy when Fantasia won on American Idol. I liked her hip-hop R&B Club feel.  She seemed like the girl that you'd watch in the middle of the dance floor going "Heeeeey."  But this album is the woman sitting at the small table in the corner with a cigarette in her mouth.  For her bubbly personality, this album was a little bitter and way too hopeless romantic.  My heart still beats fast to "Summertime", and I really enjoyed "Truth Is", "Selfish" and "Don't Act Right", but they had an up-beat dance feel to them.  "Summertime" is kinda old school but she adds a lot of flavor to it.  The rest of these songs just seem so Old School R&B.  I'm not knocking Old School R&B, but I was looking for something different in this album.  She's got a song called "Baby Mama" which congratulates women who have children and no man in their lives, who are also still doing things to improve their future regardless of dude being in their lives or not. But the rest of the cd sounds like she's chasing dude around begging him to come back or understand why he hasn't.  The concept of this album is terrible but Fantasia's voice is beautiful.  She just needs someone else to give her a new school feel.

reviewText: I have long been a fan of Taylor Swift. I admire her courage, intellect, marketing ability and acknowledgement of her status as a role model for young girls.I have to admit that I do not like every song that Miss Swift sings, and some of them even irritate me. That said, I like certain of her songs. My favorites from this album are "Speak Now", "Mean", and "Back To December". Taylor has a knack for writing songs that resonate with teenaged girls, and steps that up a notch with the signature song, Speak Now. Featuring plaintive lyrics about a impending wedding and a jilted girl, the song comes across as a bit playful and hopeful at the same time."Mean" is a sly putdown of bullies, letting young victims of bullies know that they can have the last laugh. In a soft voice accompanied by bluegrass-tinged instrumentation, Taylor delivers her blows to bullies everywhere, real and imagined."Back To December" is another of those wishful, backward-glancing analyses of love gone wrong, and Taylor delivers it with a touch of sadness and wisdom gained.If you even remotely like Taylor Swift's musical style, by all means, buy this CD. You won't be disappointed.

reviewText: I really don't remember why I bought Afterglow, I just walked into the store one day and purchased it. I am so glad I did because buying this album has opened up a whole new world of music for me, when I bought this album it led me to getting into the music of Tori Amos and Alanis Morissette. Afterglow is an amazing album, not just the title! It has some of the best songs you may ever listen to in your life. Afterglow was a huge hit for Sarah and catapulted her back into the public eye after a 6 year hiatus.Afterglow is hugely layered and sometimes McLachlan's vocals get a bit whispery. Some of the songs to many people are a tier below previous albums, however to me some of the songs are as good as the songs on Fumbling Towards Ecstasy, one of these songs is the lead single "Fallen". Fallen is without a doubt the best song on the album, it is perfect in everyway. Rarely is a song so perfect, the lyrics are complex and work amazingly well with the music which is addictive.Another song to be released from the album "World On Fire" is a beautiful song that got a GRAMMY nomination in the Music Video Category. It has a superb video, directed by Sophie Muller. This song is a charity song. The production is top-notch. "Stupid" starts off innocent but then builds into a great rock song with a superb chorus. This song is one of my favourites from this album.Many people consider "Drifting" to be the weakest track on the album, however I like it. On this album there are no weak tracks so how can it be bad? Sarah's soothing voice adds to the vigour of the song. Another of my favourites, "Train Wreck" is the song that has the honour of being the half-way mark of the album. This song is amazing. I enjoy the way the guitar blends with the piano."Push" starts off what I call the layered half of the album. While not as layered as some of the songs it has some nice vocals, superb production and a "do da da do da da..." that sounds alot like the theme song of Dawson's Creek. "Answer" reminds me of "Ice" off her 3rd album Fumbling Towards Ecstasy. It is a very emotional track that wrenches at your heart and deminds your tears."Time" is another great song off this album. It's a great song that could in my opinion win a GRAMMY. I love the lyrics on this song, they are the best on the album. The chorus is great as well. "Perfect Girl" is very layered and mysterious. It's a great track anyway. The layers really work wonders on this song. To finish the album "Dirty Little Secret" does it with wonders. The minimalistic approach works with some simple, beautiful layers.Overall, Afterglow is pure HEAVEN. All the songs are amazing and flow really well. The album has absolutely no filler tracks or songs that seem out of place. Sarahs voice is so strong on this album and she conveys all the emotions she has dealed with over the past six years into this album making it that much better to listen to. I really do hope that we don't have to wait 6 more years for her next album.

reviewText: Reasonable Doubt released in 1996....showed the world a hungry Shawn Carter....very few knew him from a verse he did on Original Flavor's "I Got Cha Open".  As the first artist off the freshly christened Rocafella label,  Jay-Z became Brooklyn's best representative overnight....his lead off single "Ain't No N***a" destroyed the air and radiowaves shared alongside femme fatale Foxy Brown.  At first listen,  you knew that Jay-Z was destined for greatness.  Reasonable Doubt enlisted memorable guest appearances,  and the lyrical prowess of Jay-Z made this an instant classic....even though 10 years later, I don't agree that Jay-Z still possesses the same lyrical greatness that caused him to skyrocket to the top of hip hop,  this album will always remain in my steady rotation.  To all of you youngsta's out there,  don't claim that Jay-Z is a legend until you hear how it all started first.

reviewText: Great record... if you resist 'cause of AMY's wretched reputation, consider it a plus... this album is the album of the decade, and it is superior.  When I say "great," I mean GREAT.  In just a few decades, or perhaps a century or two, this record may be forgotten, but right now, AMY is hot.  She has mined the great R&B, Motown Soul, British Pop, and BLUES records, and who knows what else, to create an homage to record making, and individual artistic statement in such medium, that is both monumental and personal.  With heartbreaking clarity, and gorgeous arrangements, AMY refines her soulful, R&B, Pop idiosyncratic vocals 'round these stunningly sensitive and intelligent lyrics and rich tunes that she wrote.  A rare artist's record for an artist who knew exactly what she was doing, BACK TO BLACK is a jaw-droppingly marvelous, goose-pimple raising, lovely lovingly lush indulgence with artistry to match.  This is not fashion; this is style.  AMY WINEHOUSE is one of the most incredibly talented artists I've ever listened to (and that is no small number).  I have to give this album the highest rating for being the best record of the last 10 years.

reviewText: All I knew of Leonard Cohen before I bought this album was "Suzanne" -- wonderful lyrics, with a kind of folk-song quality that nonetheless didn't sound archaic.  Why didn't I follow up?  Maybe because I was getting hooked on classical music and opera in the late '60's and early '70's.  Now that I'm in my "rediscovering my youth" phase, I try this album.  It's very very good.  As a songwriter, he has some of Dylan's verbal dexterity, but is less playful, more consistently somber.  Like Dylan too, he tends to present or imply a narrative in his songs, but sometimes he's more allusive in the way he does this this.  And like Joni Mitchell -- who must be a near contemporary -- the music seems to be what the lyrics demand, rather than melody for which words have been found.  His voice is very lovely, and while sometimes he seems to be speaking rather than singing, he is in fact singing.  He's a baritone, I would say, but when he employs the upper end of his voice, the effect is striking and powerful, as in "A Bunch of Lonesome Heroes."  This album clearly comments on Vietnam, though not directly, and I suppose it's "anti-war," but what's going on is subtler than that -- the singer seems complicit in the wrongs he is deploring, and there's guilt and regret mixed up with subdued outrage.  "Bird on a Wire" is a great song, and so is "The Partisan" and "The Old Revolution."  Of the more personal songs, "Lady Midnight" is a stunner.  No high spirits here -- but really great stuff.Follow-up:  I just found out that Joni Mitchell is almost a decade younger.  So LC's "anti-war" songs -- if that's what they are -- aren't "youthful rebellion."  He had some miles on him by 1968, though the mood of these songs suggests someone older still.

reviewText: If E.T. actually existed and if he came down to Earth and asked for a sample of Earth music, what albums would you pick? Undoubtedly, 'Thriller' would be part of the list, and not just because it was the biggest selling album of all time, with 46 million copies sold worldwide (more now with this Special Edition). Quite simply, 'Thriller' is quintessential because it combines perfect singing, perfect production, perfect songwriting, perfect dance music and perfect ballads.This doesn't mean that Michael Jackson's best work is there, far from it (though I believe "Billie Jean" to be one of the best songs of the century), and you'll find better dance numbers on 1979's 'Off The Wall' for instance. No, it's just that 'Thriller' is the perfect combination, a summary of what quality in music should be.Sure, the style is a bit dated in places ("Baby Be Mine" or "P.Y.T" and even "The Girl Is Mine" sound old!) but face it, this record will get you dancing, loving, smiling, just the way a record should. The impeccable lineup of musicians (prominently the band Toto and the Brothers Johnson) doesn't hurt either...Releasing a Special Edition should have been any fan's dream, but as it turned out, I felt a little cheated by this. First of all, there are only three bonus tracks, the rest being interview clips with Quincy Jones. Though I do not deny the value of such testimony and insight as his, it will come as no surprise to anyone if I say that there is nothing more annoying than having to skip the talking when you listen to an album. This is certainly not the kind of stuff you want to hear everytime you listen to a record! It would have been wiser to feature a bonus CD with the interview, and leave the main CD for music, if only for the sake of continuous play.Moreover, apart form the voice-over session to "Thriller" by MJJ and Vincent Price (a rare treat, which even includes a left-out verse), the other two bonus songs are incomplete: Not only "Someone In The Dark" (from the E.T. project) is just the opening version, but Quincy's voice overlaps the music's intro, and therefore the song is useless by itself; as to "Carousel" (previously known to fans as "Circus Girl"), it is a two-and-a-half minute edit version (the original recording is more than THREE-and-a-half minutes long)!Besides, the official fanclub announcement in France stated that this edition would also include the song "Starlight" (the first version of "Thriller", with different lyrics and no monsters), but this just never happened... With all the great extra songs left out from "Thriller" in 1982, such as "Nightline", "Trouble", "Can't Get Outta The Rain", "Hot Street" and even the McCartney produced, early solo version of "The Girl Is Mine", there was plenty of material for a better release than that. Or is Sony waiting for Michael's demise to capitalize on his unreleased work, of which they have tons?

It would have been wiser to feature a bonus CD with the interview, and leave the main CD for music, if only for the sake of continuous play.Moreover, apart form the voice-over session to "Thriller" by MJJ and Vincent Price (a rare treat, which even includes a left-out verse), the other two bonus songs are incomplete: Not only "Someone In The Dark&quot Quincy's voice overlaps the music's intro, and therefore the song is useless by itself; as to "Carousel" (previously known to fans as "Circus Girl"), it is a two-and-a-half minute edit version (the original recording is more than THREE-and-a-half minutes long)!Besides, the official fanclub announcement in France stated that this edition would also include the song "Starlight" (the first version of "Thriller", with different lyrics and no monsters), but this just never happened... With all the great extra songs left out from "Thriller" in 1982, such as "Nightline", "Trouble", "Can't Get Outta The Rain", "Hot Street" and even the McCartney produced, early solo version of "The Girl Is Mine", there was plenty of material for a better release than that. Or is Sony waiting for Michael's demise to capitalize on his unreleased work, of which they have tons?

reviewText: It was the late 70's and unless you lived through it, it may be kind of hard to understand. Disco ruled the radio, you couldn't turn the dial without finding the latest and greatest by the Bee Gees or The Village People. The term "Rock" was now assigned to bands like Styx or Supertramp. The guitar driven rock of Led Zep, The Who and Kiss, were pushed to the back-burner of the American music scene. Then out of nowhere Van Halen burst onto the scene. With the opening chords of "Runnin' With The Devil" into "Eruption" and "You Really Got Me", Van Halen cemented the new American rock sound. No matter what era of Van Halen you prefer, DLR vs. Sammy, it's impossible to top the band's debut album. This was something new, something purely American, and opened the door to what we know as Hard Rock or Heavy Metal today. It's impossible to listen to any rock artist today and not hear the influence of Van Halen. The 80's hair-metal scene was basically made up of bands immitating this album. Is it coincidence that soon after Van Halen debuted disco died, and bands like Twisted Sister emerged? Why bother reviewing the songs on this disk, unless you have lived under a rock for the last 25+ years you have heard each of the songs on this album at one point or another? These songs are classics, and have stood the test of time. I have owned this album on vinyl, 8-Track, cassette and CD. If you don't own this disk already.....well what are you waiting for. Like The Beatles "Sgt. Pepper", or AC/DC's "Highway to Hell" and Pink Floyd's "Dark Side of the Moon", "Van Halen" is an essenital album for your cd collection.

reviewText: This album is not the exact same style as Tragic Kingdom, but it still sounds very good.  The first song, BND, is only 45 seconds but is one of the highlights.  Actually, the last track, Brand New Day, is the elongated version of BND with added vocals.  The 2nd song Let's Get Back has undoubtebly one of the best intros ever, and is one of my favorite songs of all time.  Ache is kind of a not as serious song about a tooth ache.  Move On is the closet No Doubt comes to metal.  Doormat is a great song.  Big City Train sounds kind of strange on the first listen, but sounds great after repeated.  Sinking is most likely about alcoholism, and Trapped In A Box is about watching too much TV.  The standout of the album is the ballad Sometimes, which is beautiful.  Gwen's vocals sound perfect on the song.  If you enjoy a fun filled, carefree album with a combination of ska/pop/rock, buy this.  It's worth it!

reviewText: This CD is a nice way to get the best of what ABBA has to offer.  It is good especially if you are someone looking to add the best of what ABBA has to offer into your music library.  I usually prefer a Greatest Hits CD to be in sequential order and this does not seem to be the case with this CD.It contains all of the hits, although I would have liked to see "Eagle" and "Ring Ring" on the Gold CD.  These were included on a follow-up CD "More Abba Gold".The CD liner notes contain pictures of past ABBA albums on the inside front cover.  There are also 2 collages of ABBA photos.  John Tobler writes a very nice 5 page piece that documents the story of the band.If you are an ABBA fan or look to go deeper beyond the hits, I would recommend getting the "Thank You For the Music" box set. You may want to consider investing in this if you are even thinking of getting the follow-up "More Abba Gold" CD.  The 4 CD box set contains a more complete discography of ABBA's body of work and also contains unreleased material.
summary: Good Intro To Abba...but caution if you want to go deeper

reviewText: Uk-based trio White Lies released an intruiging (and much hyped in the UK) debut album "To Lose My Life" in 2009, which debuted at No. 1 in the UK album charts. After extensive touring now comes the second, much anticipated, sophomore album."Rituals" (10 tracks; 50 min.) starts off with "Is Love", which immediately grabs you even though it takes a bit for the song to fully explode. And we are off! "Strangers" is an equally appealing song (and obvious candidate for a single release), with up-tempo drums and underlying synthesizers. But wait! There is more! "Bigger Than Us" (first UK single) follows, and brings the band to full glory. The song is an irresistable, arena-sized stomper when it gets to the chorus, just wow. It is the best track of the album for me. Just those first three songs are worth buying the album, period. But the good tracks continue, dark and brooding and huge. The second half of the album opens with "Holy Ghost", which I just love. Things get a little less interesting towards the album, but I must tell you that I've been playing the album pretty much non-stop since getting it a few weeks ago.In all, this is clearly a step up from the debut album, and one of the best albums I've heard this year, just great. I had the good fortune of catching the band live last Fall when they were opening up for Kings of Leon, and it is clear this band is going places. "Ritual" sounds like it was made to be played in big arenas and I have no doubt that's where this band is going eventually, headlining arenas instead of opening for the likes of Kings of Leon. Highly recommended!
summary: 4.5 stars... White Lies becomes arena-sized "Bigger Than Us"

reviewText: When Slash left Guns N' Roses in 1996, many GNR fans have impatiently waited and demanded another "Appetite for Destruction". When Slash, Duff and Matt Sorum got together with Stone Temple Pilots frontman Scott Weiland to form the supergroup Velvet Revolver, there was a sigh of relief among rock fans that they will get the music that they desired for. Finally, a real hard rock band in the age of Creed and Nickelback. Of course, never mind the fact thatsome of therock bandswere alreadydelivering thatkind of musicat the time. Apparently,those guysweren'thard rockenough for these fans.Unfortunately, Velvet Revolver proved to be a failure - uninspired music, lackluster songwriting and a strong lack of chemistry between the frontman and the music players. It didn't take a brain surgeon to know that having Scott Weiland play with Slash was like havingChris Cornell work with Timbaland. So in the span of four years, Weiland was no longer in the band, everyone pursued solo projects and Velvet Revolver went into hiatus, still without a frontman to this day. The saviors of rock n' roll, ladies and gentlemen.But shortly after Weiland's departure, Slash made an announcement that he and his friends were going to create a good, old-fashioned rock n' roll album a la "Appetite", one that he was unable to make during his final days with Axl Rose. And since Axl didn't deliver that kind of album, many fans point their hopes on Slash to deliver a worthy successor to that towering masterpiece of hard rock. It also helped that Slash recruited some of the best and best-loved icons of rock, - the lead singer of Motorhead, the prince of darkness Ozzy Osbourne, the alternative rock gods Chris Cornell and Dave Grohl, the godfather of punk Iggy Pop - some newcomers such as Black Eyed Peas vocalist Fergie, Maroon 5 lead singer Adam Levine and Avenged Sevenfold singer M. Shadows - and, most of all, the three former members of GNR. Seriously, how could it all go wrong?Well, everything - music, lyrics, creativity, production. Moreso than the Velvet Revolver albums, there is not an ounce of inspiration and creativity in these fourteen lackluster tracks. Most of these songs are boring rehashes of 80s hard rock cliches, some that were best forgotten. How depressing is it to hear the likes of Ozzy Osbourne, Iggy Pop, Kid Rock and Chris Cornell waste their considerable gifts in singing such hackneyed, trite lyrics? How discouraging is it that given the talent involved, you're left feeling empty and unfulfilled? Think about it for a second - you have an album by Slash that consists of Dave Grohl, Iggy Pop, Ozzy Osbourne, Chris Cornell, Kid Rock, Lemmy, Fergie and the three former members of Guns N' Roses - and it still blew. Imagine "A Momentary Lapse of Reason" replacing David Gilmour with Slash and you pretty much got the picture.I wanted so badly to like this album, but I came out of it feeling short-changed. When not even Izzy Stradlin could take a dull hard rocker like "Ghosts" and bring it to life, you know you're in trouble. Unfortunately, that's just the tip of the iceberg. Most of the other tracks are guilty of bad quality, starting with "Crucify the Dead", which may rank as one of Ozzy Osbourne's worst vocal performances. A lifeless power ballad where the Ozzman takes a blatant shot at Axl Rose ("A gun jammed with a rose". How original), "Crucify the Dead" is proof that the Prince of Darkness and sentimentality do not mix. The next track "Beautiful Dangerous", featuring Fergie, is better, but not much. Fergie is in good form, but she's no match for the song's ridiculous lyrics ("And that's when I spin on the pole/Now my head's exploding and your gun is loaded/So I'm guessing I'm on a roll" What the hell?) and sludge of processed guitar riffs and bland keyboards. I thought this was a good, old-fashioned rock n' roll album?The rest of the tracks are hardly "Smooth" with Rob Thomas. "Back From Cali" is cut-rate AC/DC rip-off featuring the ever-derivative Myles Kennedy sounding like a haphazard cross of Bruce Dickinson, Geddy Lee and Robert Plant. "I Hold On", feat. Kid Rock, is a retread of far superior Kid Rock ballads such as "Lonely Road of Faith", "Picture" and "Cold and Empty". "Promise", feat. Chris Cornell, sounds like a weakly crafted demo from the Soundgarden basement. and "Nothing to Say" begins as a promising Sabbath-like epic, but disintegrates into a tedious speed metal track featuring forced singing by the usually talented M. Shadows.The most tolerable songs on this album are "Gotten" feat. Adam Levine; "Doctor Alibi" feat. Lemmy; and the instrumental "Watch This Dave", with appearances by Duff McKagan and drummer Dave Grohl. The former is a warm love song where Adam Levine brings life to half-baked lyrics and the latter two tracks have a momentum and fervent energy that is sadly missing from the rest of the album. Depressingly, these songs would be considered expendable in these artists' music catalogs.The greatest disappointment, however, is the production. For an album aspiring to be like "Appetite for Destruction", I have never heard such a clean, polished sound.  If it was raw, sloppily produced a la "New York Dolls", "Raw Power" or "In Utero", perhaps the album's music would probably sound better than it is, but the refined Eric Valentine and Big Chris Flores production really suck the life out of these songs, making the songs' deficiencies more blatant and obvious.As stated earlier, I wanted to like this album a lot; my love for Guns N' Roses is immeasurable. Unfortunately, albums like "Slash" prove that what these band members couldn't do alone what they did together. Despite the star-studded cast, "Slash" failed to make a dent at the Billboard charts and the gap of talent between Slash and Axl more obvious. Slash is an extremely talented guitarist, but without a songwriter like Axl or even Izzy, he's lost in making hackneyed mediocrities like this.If Slash wants to get cozy with his buddies and play uninspired rehashes of "Nightrain", "Sweet Child O'Mine" or "Locomotive", then he's welcome to it. Unfortunately, this album will only serve as an unintentional reminder that no matter what kind of person he was, Axl Rose was clearly the writer.Far from being "Supernatural", Slash's solo album is a super bore.Strong recommendation to avoid.
summary: You wanted another "Appetite"? Well, it's here and it sucks

reviewText: As the title I gave to my review says, to me "The Sound of Revenge" and Chamillionaire himself are a breath of fresh air for the rap game, and a much needed one at that! It's not a secret that the South has been running the game for the last few years, as many rappers from Atlanta and Houston came up blew up, continuing the legacy of the vets before them... However, many people, including myself, felt that many of those new rappers from the South don't say much really. It seems like they prefer to rap about candy paints and cadillac grills, very unlike the vets before them (such as Scarface, The Geto Boys, Tela, Eightball & MJG, UGK and others)... Especially with Lil' Jon making the crunk sound, where all you need to actually do is scream like an idiot over a thumping beat and you got yourself a hit...And here comes Chamillionaire. Bringing something new to the South Rap Game. Changing the game actually. As most of you probably know, Chamillionaire started with Paul Wall, also being a part of the Swisha House project...However they split up, and Chamillionaire started focusing on releasing some of his classic mixtapes ("The Truth", "Mixtape Massiah", "Chamillitary" etc), untill he got signed by Universal, who could see his obvious talent, feeling that Cham (born Hakeem Sariki) could be much more than a mixtape rapper, using other people's beats...And Universal got it right. Because Chamillionaire IS different. And better. And you can see it over this masterpiece of an album. While his former partner Paul Wall picked up the torch for diamonds and flossing and ran with it, without expanding his range of topics, Cham has steadily showed an increasing depth far beyond talking about wealth. He's become adept at punchlines, worked hard on mastering the craft of storytelling, and lightened up his flow and diction in general. Cham flows like a lyrical Swiss watch - flawless timing. And without trying so hard to sound "southern" and emphasising a southern accent. Cham just flows every way he feels like it - sometimes he flows as fast as a Bone Thug Member, and sometimes he slows it down. Another thing that separated Cham, other than the things mentioned above, is Chamillionaire's hooks. The guy is just a genius at creating those catchy hooks...And you know what? He SINGS them. You may say Cham looks a bit like 50 Cent (another rapper who TRIES to sing on his hooks), but hey, King Koopa does his singing VERY WELL. Yes, you read this well - he can sing, and it's obvious on every one of his hooks, he's got a very good voice and singing delivery (unlike all those rappers who try to sing and go it wack- such as 50 Cent, Andre 3000, Pharnell, Snoop Dogg and the list goes on). I think the only rapper that sings better than Cham is Krayzie Bone, but Krayzie is in a league of his own anyway...  So, the hooks are extremely nice and catchy and with Cham doing them, it shows you how versatile this guy is!...Another thing that makes Chamillionaire and this album special is the content of the songs. Cham doesn't rap about fancy cars, diamond watches or about killing people and selling drugs. He raps about himself, about his life or life in general, or just about other topics that are very different than any of those new Southern cats rap about. On "Snitchin" he raps about the code of the srteets and snitches. On "Frontin" he confronts all those fake gangstas... On "Rain" Chamillionaire raps about strugles of life, but not about the hood, but about struggles of life in general, in a way thay ANYWAY can feel it, not only guys who live in the hood. On the hit single "Ridin" he raps about crooked policemen, who always try to find dirt on you... and the list goes on. What I am trying to say, that every song is about SOMETHING. There are no songs without a topic where you hear the rapper just rapping about unrelated stuff. Each song has it's own topic and Cham stays with it.The production on the album is flawless, and perfect. Cham got some big names producing for him (Scott Storch, Mannie Fresh and Cool&Dre...; THANKS, GOD, NO LIL' JON BEATS!!) but most of the album is produced by less known producers who do a tremendous job, especially the Beat Bullies, whose beats are just amazing.So, the bottom line is, that this album is different. Chamillionaire's rapping and lyrical content is special and unique, his singing is impressive, the hooks are extremely catchy, and the beats are flawless. And if THAT's not enough, the album features some great  guest artists (Scarface, Krayzie Bone, Bun B, Lil' Wayne, Rasaq, singer Natalie, Killer Mike, Pastor Troy and a few others).If you never felt the "new" South movement, Chamillionaire is the answer for you. He brings something entire new to the table, and this talent should not be overlooked.

reviewText: The Streets (Mike Skinner) is one of my favorite artists around.  He's very original, hard-to-categorize, and doesn't sound like a lot of other hiphop acts.This CD is yet another solid album beginning to end.  It's not quite as good as A Grand..., which was a great day-in-the-life-of concept album, but this one's still great.  I could see if you were a die-hard rap fan who only listened to rap, you might not like this guy.The Streets always covers diverse topics (ie, missing his dead dad); he's one of the 'realest' rappers out there, not afraid to reveal his emotions and personal life.The beats are actually decent, with more electro influences.  The beats are still simple.  The Streets is definitely not all about great beats; it's always been about Mike's rapping/talking.  Luckily that format hasn't changed at all.This is a very solid album.  My biggest complaint is that it's too short at 11 songs 37 minutes long.  Recommended to fans of his previous work.

reviewText: I REALLY wanted to give this album one more star, but I just couldn't. The material here is as great as ever, with nine gems and only one song that's merely okay ("Welcome To Try"). But some of Gordon's weakest vocal performances are here, with a voice that sounds alternately strained and lazy. He seems to be either exhausted or struggling with laryngitis. The smoothest vocal is probably the first one, "Restless", which is a warm, lonely ballad with some distant strings and cool effects.Speaking of effects, I noticed that Lightfoot himself is listed as a producer on this project. He seems to prefer an almost bare-bones approach; "Less is more", as they say. You know how sometimes it just feels right to eat fruit salad instead of chocolate cheesecake? This album is kinda like that. Most of the time it works, although I can't help thinking it might have sold better if the presentation were a tad more elaborate. "Only Love Would Know" in particular, gives the impression of a project that was never quite finished. There's a piece of the studio demo vocal track near the end of the song, probably intended as a reference for some sweet backup vocals that were never added. I'm amazed that no one at WB prevented the song from being released in such an unprofessional condition. And it's a shame, because it's a charming little romantic ballad, worthy of a first-class treatment.Standout tunes include "Restless", "Fading Away", "Only Love Would Know" and "Wild Strawberries." For me, a huge Lightfoot fan, the quality of the material makes it more than worth the cost of the album, even if I cringe at the vocals now and then.Certainly, no fan should be without it. I'm hoping someday he might record some of these again and give them the royal treatment they deserve.

reviewText: I remember the 80's with rock stars with the big teased long hair, the earrings, pastel loud colors (and that's just the men/male rock groups for starters). Van Halen during this time represented why a lot of young guys musically inclined had dreams of becoming rock stars and making it big some day... While many fans and critics hailed Van Halen for being a good old American metal or hard rock band I always thought the original lineup was inventive and innovative. Not many groups of the time could combine synth-technology with real drums and electric guitars; They could. 1984 proved they could and did with great finesse and success.Still love that drum intro-solo to Hot For Teacher (as well as the video). The other amazing and noteworthy underlying element was David Lee Roth's rock/soul throaty vocals which lended an underlying & faint blues-like sound (remember his solo effort and the re-make single I'm Just a Gigolo)...Despite it's commercial overplay on radio back then it has remained as one of my all time favorite Van Halen albums not to be repeated again by them or any other group trying to imitate them...By the way commendations to the artist for the album cover of the airbrushed cherub smoking the cigarettes;It's one of the more memorable and excellent album concept art covers for the decade (maybe 20th century) !...

These 10- to 12-track releases are no longer acceptable.

reviewText: Orginally released in 1968, The Songs of Leonard Cohen was an album like nothing else comming out at that time. Then again, Leonard Cohen is artist like no one else before him. This was a time when political cynicism was echoed in the lyrics of Country Joe's Super Bird, (an ode to LBJ) and Dylan's Rainy Day Woman tested the airwaves with the refrain "everybody must get stoned".So what was it about the ultra-cool Canadian with the stoic attitude and monotone voice that was so captivating? To begin with the songs were plaintive, desperate, at times almost suicidal. The deeply religious overtones added to the mystery of the entire experience. In short this collection of poems was so profound, I can remember listening to it almost exclusively for three or four months. Even today, when I play The Songs of Leonard Cohen, I become so engrossed, so enraptured, that I drop everything and have to listen to it in its entirety, without interruption. I honestly can't say that about any other album.

reviewText: Along with almost every teenager I know, The Used's self titled CD is one of my personal favorites. I think it's because no one had heard of anything quite like The Used or anyone else in the "screamo" genre. Often it's hard to be better and beat the sophomore jinx (think 50 Cent, off the top of my head) but In Love and Death is an excellent effort. It took me a little while to warm up and it felt like forever till they put it out, but the wait was worth it. What I like is that they always incorporate different influences in the music. For example, certain songs have almost a blues-y feeling to them (Cut Up Angels, Yesterday's Feelings), yet songs like Take it Away and Sound Effects and Overdramatics seem harder than other songs on their debut. So if you want my opinion, which I know you do, pick this CD up. If not for yourself, then your kids (if you have any) will probably dig it.

reviewText: This is The Time. Make no mistake about it. It's the original seven members reunited on album for the first in a long. What's disappointing is the new name, which they apparently had to adopt because Prince, who created the band in 1981; this is their first album he has no artistic involvement in; owns the original name and doesn't want to let them use it anymore. Now they're The Original Seven; a change that wouldn't be nearly as atrocious if it weren't for the way they decided to stylize the word "Seven". "7ven", which to me looks like Seven Ven, makes no sense.If, however, you can ignore that fatal flaw, the band is still "cool". Jimmy Jam and Terry Lewis have become perhaps my favorite music duo, thanks mainly to all the impressive songs they've made with Janet Jackson over the years, and lead singer Morris Day is as funny and charismatic as he ever was. He's 54 years old now, but his girls don't seem to age. So when the playboy partakes in a Role Play session to a relentlessly funky dance beat, the voice of the girl he's doing it with adds to the song a pretty and sexy allure. It's no wonder he has a problem being Faithful to just one.One of the few songs not to or about girls is Trendin, though it is off-putting hearing these old-schoolers; who, at one point, suggest splitting the album into two sides like a cassette tape; latch-on to such a right now (Twitter) term. The title, as they put it, even begins with a hashtag. I guess that kind of stylization, like the spelling of the new name, comes from their quirky Prince roots. But they need to give it up and perhaps focus on making better songs. This set is fun; even the mediocre songs are funked-up with dazzling highlights; but it isn't as hot as the title suggests.marcellee.com

reviewText: I feel like a Brazilian playboy with millions everytime I play this CD. I can't explain it. These are so smooth and sophisticated arrangements by Jobin, they are especially good on hot, sultry afternoons. If you like Brazilian tempos with lush arrangements, this is your cup of cappucino. The only knock is that the CD comes in around 30 mintes. In the words of the Andrea True Connection when she asked "how do you like it?" ..I say "More..More...More.." This is excellent late 60's playboy lounge music. Yes, I'll have a cocktail...shaken, not stirred.

reviewText: from Bruce at this stage of his career. If you're hoping to hear the Springsteen of old with the passion and creativity so prevalent on his first 6 albums you will be very disappointed. If you want to hear memorable contributions from Clarence Clemons and other members of the band you will again be disappointed.  If you want to hear a pretty decent album and take bruce for what he is at this stage of his career (after over 30 years of giving it everything he had), then you will enjoy this cd. Although there are really no bad songs on this cd (remarkable for a 15 track cd), there aren't any that will blow you away either. The most compelling songs are "Lonesome Day"(nice violin touch with a powerful chord structure), "Into The Fire"(you can feel it in your heart), "Empty Sky"(Bruce conveys the isolation perfectly), "Worlds Apart"(the most creative and powerful song on the cd), "Let's Be Friends"(borderline corn but Bruce pulls it off), "Your Missing"(very moving), and "The Rising"(traditional Springsteen). The worst song is "Countin' On A Miracle"(forgettable) and "My City Of Ruins" is much better than the deplorable version from the "Tribute" cd. I gave this cd 4 and a half stars not because it was a really great cd but because it was an honest effort from Springsteen to produce quality, meaningful music rather than hacking something out and selling it on his name and I appreciate that. So if you're a Springsteen fan you should buy this cd with the appropriate expectations. If you're not a Springsteen fan already this cd probably won't turn you into one. ...

reviewText: The Corrs' a smudge on the American music scene? I beg to differ considering the obscene amount of [stuff] that pollutes the airwaves from teen pop to nu metal (the new generation of hair metal). I have been a long time fan of The Corrs for several years now. I wasn't really sure whether I wanted to get a live album from The Corrs since: a) I'm not a fan of live albums and b)I own all of their songs. What got to change my mind about this album is the number of cover songs the band did, particularly my favorite Rolling Stones song "Ruby Tuesday". I also particularly loved "Summer Wine", one of the two duets Andrea did with U2's Bono. Now I'm certainly no fan of Bono (or his band for that matter) but he sounded wonderful on that song as well as the Ryan Adams' song "When the Stars Go Blue". The instrumental cover of "Little Wing" with Ron Wood on lead guitar was wonderful. Just stunning. I'm glad that two of my personal favorite Corrs songs were included in this performance, "Breathless" and "So Young". Now while I think this album and performance was albeit too short, forty-five minutes long, I thought it was well worth the money. It was interesting to hear The Corrs perform a few new cover songs. I'm rather glad they didn't play their version of Fleetwood Mac's "Dreams". That song is rather played out and tiresome to listen to. The Corrs remain a favorite pop band of mine. This live album is a good appetizer while waiting for a new studio album from the Irish quartet.
summary: Too short but excellent live album
